CLOSURE: Cross-Channel Closure for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection

DOI: XXXXXXX.XXXXXXXConference: Make sure to enter the correct conference title from your rights confirmation email; June 03–05, 2018; Woodstock, NYISBN: 978-1-4503-XXXX-X/2018/06CCS: Computing methodologies Anomaly detectionCCS: Computing methodologies Learning latent representationsCCS: Computing methodologies Neural networks
Fan Xu Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, Anhui, China email: markxu@mail.ustc.edu.cn , Hao Wu Affiliation: Tsinghua University, Beijing, China email: wu-h25@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn , Zhi Song Affiliation: City University of Hong Kong, Hongkong, China email: songzhics@gmail.co , Hanbo Huang Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China email: hhuang417@sjtu.edu.cn , Wenzhuo Ma Affiliation: Tianjin University, Tianjin, China email: 3353147727j@gmail.com , Nan Wang Affiliation: Beijing Jiaotong University, Beijing, China email: wangnanbjtu@bjtu.edu.cn , Wei Gong Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, Anhui, China email: weigong@ustc.edu.cn and Xibin Zhao Affiliation: Tsinghua University, Beijing, China email: zxb@tsinghua.edu.cn
2018
Abstract.

Multivariate time series produced by industrial installations and server clusters are under continuous monitoring, and anomaly detection is the first line of defense before a local fault escalates into a system-wide failure. In the absence of labels, the dominant paradigm trains a reconstruction model on normal data and scores the residual to reach a verdict. Recent work has steadily enriched the expressiveness of the recovery map through Transformers, diffusion models, and cross-scale associations. A residual, however, only certifies that an observation can be recovered; it does not certify that the variables still explain one another as they do under normal operation. A coordinated yet unfamiliar operating transition inflates the residual without breaking any relationship, whereas a sensor drifting away from its peers may leave the residual silent. Methods that fold inter-variable dependencies into the reconstruction objective inherit this ambiguity, because their relational evidence is ultimately supervised by the same recovery loss. We therefore propose CLOSURE, which evaluates recoverability and cross-channel consistency as two normal-data prediction tasks learned in separation. The recoverability task is solved by a diffusion reconstructor conditioned on a discrete memory of normal temporal bases. The consistency task is solved by a relation-closure operator that predicts every channel exclusively from the others, where the target’s own trajectory is withheld and sparse signed gates decide which peers are actually used. The two scores are reconciled only through calibration on normal data. Extensive experiments show that CLOSURE consistently outperforms recent reconstruction-, frequency-, and topology-based detectors on public benchmark streams, confirming the value of examining consistency alongside recoverability.

Keywords: 
Multivariate Time Series, Anomaly Detection

1. Introduction

Multivariate time series produced by industrial installations and server clusters are under continuous monitoring, and anomaly detection is the first line of defense before a local fault escalates into a system-wide failure (Tuli et al., 2022; Su et al., 2019). Labeled failures are scarce and never enumerate the ways a system can break, so detectors are typically fitted to normal observations alone. Reconstruction supplies the canonical objective for this setting: learn to reproduce normal windows, then read the residual as evidence of departure. Recurrent latent models and adversarial autoencoders established the paradigm (Su et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2019); Transformers widened the temporal context (Tuli et al., 2022); diffusion models recover observations through denoising and imputation (Zhang et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2023; Xiao et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025b); and cross-scale reconstruction with shared cross-window context further enriches what a model can recover (Li et al., 2025a). These advances strengthen the representation of normal behavior. Whether they strengthen detection depends on a separate question: how faithfully reconstruction difficulty tracks abnormality.

Reconstruction difficulty and abnormality need not coincide. Consider a healthy operating transition in which several sensors change together while preserving their usual coordination. The trajectory may be unfamiliar to the reconstructor and yield a large residual even though no channel relationship has been violated. The converse is equally plausible. A drifting sensor may follow a smooth curve that the model reproduces accurately, while it quietly stops tracking the channels with which it normally varies. Figure 1 contrasts these possibilities. They separate two properties of a single window, recoverability and cross-channel consistency, and expose an ambiguity in the residual: agreement with a learned reconstructor does not by itself establish agreement with normal relations.

Dependencies already play an important role in anomaly detection. Learned sensor graphs and inter-metric embeddings model interactions among variables (Deng and Hooi, 2021; Li et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2024). CATCH learns channel interactions inside frequency patches (Wu et al., 2025), and ScatterAD couples temporal and topological views (Yin et al., 2025). A related line uses temporal association discrepancies as detection evidence (Xu et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2023). These methods establish the value of relational evidence. Our question is therefore not whether dependencies matter, but where their supervision comes from. When inter-variable dependencies are folded into the reconstruction objective, the relational evidence is ultimately shaped by the same recovery loss, and the resulting score inherits the ambiguity above. Such a reference also needs a criterion of its own for deciding which relations enter it. A strong association within one normal interval may reflect a temporary operating condition, and a merely strong correlation does not identify the peers that a nonlinear predictor should actually use. Turning these associations directly into prediction weights therefore grants uncertain relations an influence on detection before their usefulness has been measured. We instead ask how to construct a cross-channel reference whose supervision, and whose selection of relations, are both established by a prediction task separate from reconstruction.

According to these, we introduce CLOSURE, a detector that evaluates recoverability and cross-channel consistency as two normal-data prediction tasks learned in separation. The consistency task is carried by a relation-closure operator. Each target receives nonlinear messages from its peers through learned signed coefficients and sparse gates, and never from itself; the disagreement between the observed channels and their peer predictions forms a closure residual (Batson and Royer, 2019). Because a sustained departure can raise a window’s residual background together with its endpoint, we score the endpoint relative to that background, which makes the criterion sensitive to a localized change in coordination. The recoverability task is carried by a diffusion reconstructor conditioned on a discrete memory of normal temporal bases (Li et al., 2025b). The relation operator is neither an input to this reconstructor nor a target of its training loss, and the two paths meet only after their scores are calibrated on normal data. This separation lets us hold the reconstructor fixed and vary the relational criterion alone, so that a change in detection is attributable to relation learning rather than to improved recovery. In summary, we make the following key contributions:

  • ❶

    Decoupled scoring. We formulate a detector that evaluates temporal recoverability alongside cross-channel consistency, keeping the relational reference outside the reconstruction objective and combining the two paths only at the decision stage.

  • ❷

    Learned sparse closure. We instantiate the relational criterion with signed coefficients, per-edge gates, and source-only nonlinear messages, and show that row normalization erases absolute relation strength, motivating a separate gate parameter for selection.

  • ❸

    Controlled evaluation. We prove that a target-only perturbation enters the closure residual unattenuated, and experiments with a frozen reconstructor show that learned relational evidence improves affiliation F1 beyond reconstruction alone.

2. Related Work

2.1. Reconstruction-Based Detection

Reconstruction-based detectors learn normal dynamics and score deviations through reconstruction error or likelihood. Recurrent models, adversarial autoencoders, and Transformers provide different temporal representations for this task (Su et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2019; Tuli et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2025). Diffusion approaches formulate recovery as conditional imputation (Chen et al., 2023; Xiao et al., 2023). PhysDiff (Li et al., 2025b) conditions corruption and attention on decomposed temporal bases, while CrossAD (Li et al., 2025a) reconstructs fine-scale observations from coarser views and shares context across windows. These designs enrich what a model can recover the residual. however, they still report agreement with a single recovery map.

2.2. Dependency Modeling

Dependencies can guide signal modeling or become detection targets. GDN (Deng and Hooi, 2021) and InterFusion (Li et al., 2021) encode channel interactions through sensor graphs and hierarchical representations, respectively. CATCH (Wu et al., 2025) learns frequency-dependent channel masks, whereas MSCRED (Zhang et al., 2019) reconstructs multiscale inter-sensor signature matrices and scores their residuals. Another line examines temporal associations through association discrepancy and dual-attention contrastive learning (Xu et al., 2021; Audibert et al., 2020; Park et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2023). ScatterAD (Yin et al., 2025) models temporal-node scattering and aligns temporal and topological representations. Across these designs, the relational evidence is produced within the reconstruction or representation objective, so its reference and the recovery map are shaped by the same loss.

2.3. Normality Constraints and Scoring

Normal references and constraints on the recovery map address the risk of accurately reconstructing anomalies. MemAE (Gong et al., 2019) retrieves normal latent prototypes for decoding, and vector quantization provides a discrete representation for such prototypes (Van Den Oord et al., 2017). MEMTO (Song et al., 2023) extends memory-guided reconstruction with latent-memory deviations that weight reconstruction errors, demonstrating that a normal reference can also supply an additional scoring criterion. IGAD (Sun et al., 2025) instead imposes idempotency and tightness losses on the reconstruction map. These constraints act on the recovery map or on the representation it decodes from, and their criterion is still read from how well the observation is reproduced.

These methods use learned dynamics, dependencies, or normal prototypes to define detection evidence. CLOSURE instead complements reconstruction with a relational reference that is learned separately and never enters the reconstruction objective. Its signed closure operator evaluates whether observed channels remain mutually explainable when each target is withheld from its own prediction, rather than reconstructing a relation matrix or measuring distance to a latent prototype.

3. Methodology

Problem setup. Let xt∈ℝDx_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} contain the retained channels of a multivariate series and Xt=[xt−L+1,…,xt]⊤∈ℝL×DX_{t}=[x_{t-L+1},\ldots,x_{t}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times D} its length-LL window. We seek a score ata_{t} for the observed endpoint, using normal data for fitting and calibration. The normal sequence is divided chronologically into training 𝒩tr\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{tr}}, validation 𝒩val\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{val}}, and calibration 𝒩cal\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cal}}. Windows stay within their assigned segments, with L−1L-1 unused timestamps between segments. All inputs use training-fitted scaling.

Overview. Figure 2 follows one window through two paths that answer different questions. ❶ Temporal reconstruction measures how accurately a learned model recovers XtX_{t} given normal temporal context. ❷ Relational closure measures whether the channels of XtX_{t} remain mutually explainable under a learned normal relation reference. Three components are fitted separately: a discrete basis codec, the reconstructor, and the relation predictor. The relation path receives neither memory codes nor reconstruction outputs, and contributes no gradient to them. Both paths are frozen at detection and meet only through normal-calibrated scoring.

3.1. Memory-Conditioned Temporal Reconstruction

The reconstruction path measures how accurately an entire window can be recovered from normal temporal context, and reports the resulting discrepancy at the observed endpoint. We introduce the basis-conditioned diffusion backbone and represent the normal bases with learned discrete codecs, so that recovery is conditioned on stored normal patterns rather than on the test window itself.

A discrete normal basis memory. High- and low-frequency bases are extracted from normal training windows by adaptive multicomponent decomposition. For band u∈{h,l}u\in\{h,l\}, channel-wise bases are split into length-pp patches, normalized by training-fitted scales, and quantized against a codebook 𝒞u={cku}k=1K\mathcal{C}_{u}=\{c^{u}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} through a straight-through estimator (Van Den Oord et al., 2017):

Each band owns a codec shared across channels. A memory slot stores the paired code-index sequences of one normal template; reading a slot decodes both bands and restores channel scales to give ℬ=(Bh,Bl)\mathcal{B}=(B^{h},B^{l}) with Bu∈ℝL×DB^{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times D}. The scored channel set is fixed independently of the gates, so closing a row’s connections changes the predictor without removing that target from evaluation. The ratio isolates a localized change in coordination; a departure sustained across the window raises numerator and background alike, so this score does not measure anomaly duration.

Separate prediction objectives. Normal windows supervise both paths, but the two objectives update disjoint parameters:

+λ​𝒮​(α),\displaystyle+\lambda\mathcal{S}(\alpha),

The codec is frozen before the reconstructor is trained, and ℒrel\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rel}} sends no gradient to θ\theta or the codec. Every target contributes to the Huber loss even when all of its incoming gates close, so pruning cannot lower the objective by dropping a difficult target. Normal validation selects both checkpoints, by reconstruction error for θ\theta and by deterministic unpenalized Huber loss for (ϕ,α)(\phi,\alpha).

Normal-calibrated decision. The two errors share no scale. Each is standardized by its own branch statistics on 𝒩cal\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cal}} and passed through softplus to give nonnegative evidence, and the fused score is their equal-weight mean:

Parameters, score transforms, and hh stay fixed at test time, and labels enter evaluation only, without point adjustment. This quantile is an operating point, not a guarantee of false-alarm control under distribution shift.

3.4. Theoretical Analysis

Both statements concern the frozen operator G⋆G^{\star} in fixed standardized coordinates, before the endpoint ratio of Eq. 8. The first identifies what the architectural restriction guarantees, the second which perturbations the residual can expose.

Theorem 3.2 (Target-excluded closure response).

Let E⁡(Z)=Z−G⋆​(Z)E(Z)=Z-G^{\star}(Z) and let eie_{i} be the iith coordinate vector. For any target ii and trajectory perturbation δ∈ℝL\delta\in\mathbb{R}^{L},

(11) [G⋆(Z+δei⊤)]:,i=[G⋆(Z)]:,i,E(Z+δei⊤):,i−E(Z):,i=δ.\bigl[G^{\star}(Z+\delta e_{i}^{\top})\bigr]_{:,i}=\bigl[G^{\star}(Z)\bigr]_{:,i},\quad E(Z+\delta e_{i}^{\top})_{:,i}-E(Z)_{:,i}=\delta.
Proof.

By Eq. 7, every message entering target ii is a function of zjz_{j} with j≠ij\neq i only, and the frozen coefficients and deterministic gates are input-independent. Perturbing ziz_{i} thus leaves [G⋆(Z)]:,i[G^{\star}(Z)]_{:,i} unchanged; subtracting it gives the residual identity. ∎

No linearity is assumed: ψϕ\psi_{\phi} is nonlinear, but no source of target ii is ziz_{i}. A target-only change therefore enters the signed residual undiminished, and cannot be absorbed by copying the target. Absolute error need not grow, since a perturbation may cancel an existing residual.

Changes explained by peers. For a general perturbation Δ\Delta, let U⁡(Z,Δ)=Δ−[G⋆​(Z+Δ)−G⋆​(Z)]U(Z,\Delta)=\Delta-[G^{\star}(Z+\Delta)-G^{\star}(Z)] be the part of the change the predictor fails to reproduce, with mean absolute magnitudes ℛ⁡(Z)=‖E⁡(Z)‖1,1/(L​D)\mathcal{R}(Z)=\left\lVert E(Z)\right\rVert_{1,1}/(LD) and 𝒟⁡(Z,Δ)=‖U⁡(Z,Δ)‖1,1/(L​D)\mathcal{D}(Z,\Delta)=\left\lVert U(Z,\Delta)\right\rVert_{1,1}/(LD). Since E⁡(Z+Δ)=E⁡(Z)+U⁡(Z,Δ)E(Z+\Delta)=E(Z)+U(Z,\Delta) requires no linearity, the reverse triangle inequality in both orders gives:

(12) |ℛ⁡(Z+Δ)−𝒟⁡(Z,Δ)|≤ℛ⁡(Z),|ℛ⁡(Z+Δ)−ℛ⁡(Z)|≤𝒟⁡(Z,Δ).\bigl|\mathcal{R}(Z+\Delta)-\mathcal{D}(Z,\Delta)\bigr|\leq\mathcal{R}(Z),\quad\bigl|\mathcal{R}(Z+\Delta)-\mathcal{R}(Z)\bigr|\leq\mathcal{D}(Z,\Delta).

When normal closure is small, the first bound places ℛ⁡(Z+Δ)\mathcal{R}(Z+\Delta) near the unexplained part of the change, and the two together give 𝒟⁡(Z,Δ)>2​ℛ​(Z)⇒ℛ⁡(Z+Δ)>ℛ⁡(Z)\mathcal{D}(Z,\Delta)>2\mathcal{R}(Z)\Rightarrow\mathcal{R}(Z+\Delta)>\mathcal{R}(Z). Conversely, a coordinated change the peers reproduce keeps 𝒟\mathcal{D} small and the residual near its original value, however large ‖Δ‖\left\lVert\Delta\right\rVert. Neither direction requires the reconstruction error to move, which is what makes the branches non-redundant.

4. Experiments

4.1. Experimental Settings

Benchmarks. We evaluate CLOSURE on five real-world multivariate time series datasets. (i) MSL is public data released from NASA (Hundman et al., 2018), which contain the telemetry anomaly data derived from the Incident Surprise Anomaly reports of spacecraft monitoring systems. (ii) SWaT (Mathur and Tippenhauer, 2016) originates from a critical infrastructure system under 11 days of continuous operations with 51 sensors. (iii) PSM (Abdulaal et al., 2021) is collected internally from diverse application server nodes from eBay. (iv) SMD (Su et al., 2019) is a five-week-long dataset released from a large Internet company. (v) SMAP (Hundman et al., 2018) contains spacecraft telemetry and anomaly annotations from NASA’s Soil Moisture Active Passive mission. We additionally consider two NeurIPS-TS scenarios used by PhysDiff (Li et al., 2025b): (vi) GECCO, named Water in the local release, records nine sensor variables from a water-monitoring system, including pH, temperature, and conductivity. (vii) Creditcard contains 29 transaction features with rare fraudulent transactions marked as anomalies, extending the benchmark scope to financial fraud detection. For fairness, we split all datasets into training 𝒩tr\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{tr}}, validation 𝒩val\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{val}}, and calibration 𝒩cal\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cal}} in a 70%/15%/15%70\%/15\%/15\% ratio.

Baselines. We conduct a comparative analysis of CLOSURE against 16 baselines for comprehensive evaluations, including (i) the classic methods: LOF (Breunig et al., 2000), iForest (Liu et al., 2012); (ii) prediction-based methods: CL-MPPCA (Tariq et al., 2019), TimesNet (Wu et al., 2022), MTAD-GAT (Zhao et al., 2020); (iii) reconstruction-based methods: LSTM-VAE (Park et al., 2018), BeatGAN (Zhou et al., 2019), InterFusion (Li et al., 2021), OmniAnomaly (Su et al., 2019). Then, from the pespective of model architecture, we compare our model with: (iv) Transformer-based methods: Anomaly Transformer (AnoTran) (Xu et al., 2021), TranAD (Tuli et al., 2022), NPSR (Lai et al., 2024), DCdetector (Yang et al., 2023); and (v) Diffusion-based methods: DiffAD (Xiao et al., 2023), ImDiffusion (Chen et al., 2023), D3R (Wang et al., 2023).

Evaluation Metrics. To assess the detection performance of our proposed CLOSURE and the baseline models, we employ three standard metrics: affiliation precision, recall, and F1 (Huet et al., 2022), denoted Aff-P, Aff-R, and Aff-F1. These metrics measure the temporal proximity between predicted anomaly intervals and ground-truth events, with Aff-F1 defined as the harmonic mean of Aff-P and Aff-R. All values are reported as percentages, and no point adjustment is applied. To ensure statistical significance, we report the average results over five independent runs.

4.2. Main Results

4.2.1. Quantitative Results

Performance across benchmarks. Table 1 reports the highest Aff-F1 for CLOSURE among the listed methods on all five datasets. The largest margin is on SMD, where its 88.1388.13 exceeds D3R’s 78.0478.04 by 10.0910.09 percentage points. On the spacecraft datasets, CLOSURE reaches 75.2575.25 on MSL and 73.6973.69 on SMAP, exceeding the strongest respective baselines, LSTM-VAE and AnoTran, by 2.632.63 and 2.042.04 points. The gain on PSM is 1.521.52 points over ImDiffusion. SWaT presents a smaller gap: 73.0773.07 vs 72.4472.44 for DeepSVDD. The advantage in the reported F1 scores therefore spans the listed application domains, but its magnitude is dataset-dependent.

Precision–recall balance. The individual metrics reveal different operating characteristics among the methods. On SMD, iForest and AnoTran both attain 100.00100.00 precision, but their recall falls below 10.0010.00. CLOSURE combines 81.6581.65 precision with 95.7395.73 recall, avoiding this pronounced imbalance. Relative to D3R, it increases precision by 16.7816.78 percentage points while reducing recall by 2.202.20 points, resulting in a higher reported F1.

The improvements on MSL and SMAP involve increases in both metrics relative to the respective strongest F1 baselines. On MSL, CLOSURE improves precision and recall over LSTM-VAE by 1.231.23 and 5.595.59 percentage points. On SMAP, the corresponding gains over AnoTran are 1.991.99 and 1.721.72 points. On PSM, CLOSURE also improves both metrics over ImDiffusion, raising precision from 63.2763.27 to 65.2865.28 and recall from 98.6098.60 to 98.7698.76. By contrast, SWaT exhibits a precision–recall tradeoff: CLOSURE has higher precision than DeepSVDD (63.1463.14 vs 59.1159.11), alongside lower recall (86.7186.71 vs 93.5393.53).

NeurIPS-TS results. Table 2 extends the evaluation to the Creditcard and GECCO scenarios. CLOSURE achieves Aff-F1 scores of 69.4869.48 and 70.2370.23, exceeding the strongest listed baselines by 6.866.86 and 9.469.46 percentage points, respectively.

On Creditcard, CLOSURE improves over D3R in both precision (64.2764.27 vs 56.9056.90) and recall (75.6175.61 vs 69.6169.61). On GECCO, it similarly exceeds BeatGAN in precision (69.1769.17 vs 62.7162.71) and recall (71.3271.32 vs 58.9458.94), with a larger improvement in recall. In both scenarios, CLOSURE achieves the highest precision among the compared methods, while iForest attains higher recall at the cost of precision below 3.003.00. The resulting F1 comparisons reinforce the importance of jointly considering precision and recall. They also show that the advantage of CLOSURE extends to both additional scenarios without requiring it to maximize recall alone.

4.2.2. Qualitative Analysis

Figure 3 illustrates the scoring principle on a four-channel sequence. Panels (a) and (b) display the first channel in original and window-standardized coordinates, respectively, while all scores aggregate four channels. The reconstructor closely follows the observed trajectory, including the smooth deviation in the later part of the anomalous interval. Consequently, a visible departure in the trajectory does not necessarily produce a large reconstruction residual. Peer prediction departs from the observation over part of this interval, providing an additional criterion for identifying behavior that remains locally reconstructable.

The resulting responses are complementary in their temporal locations. Reconstruction scoring is most responsive to the earlier fluctuations, whereas relational scoring contributes additional alarms during the later departure. This distinction illustrates how agreement with a reconstructed trajectory and agreement with a relational reference can expose different aspects of the same anomalous interval.

Panel (c) shows how these responses combine after normal-data calibration. Reconstruction and relation scoring detect 3939 and 4444 anomalous points, respectively, with 1010 shared detections. Equal-weight fusion detects 5858 anomalous points, exceeding the individual branches by 1919 and 1414 points. The limited overlap between branch detections is consistent with the two criteria providing complementary information.

Fusion nevertheless operates on scores rather than on the union of binary alarms. The branch detections have a union of 7373 anomalous points, exceeding the 5858 detected by fusion, so some points detected by individual branches are not retained. Moreover, fusion is applied before normalization by its own calibrated threshold, and its displayed curve is therefore not the mean of the two normalized branch curves. Normal-point alarms also increase from 11 for either branch to 22 for fusion. The example thus illustrates how complementary responses can improve anomalous-point detection while retaining both missed detections and false alarms.

4.3. Mechanism Analysis

We hold observations fixed and perturb only their relational reference. Rewiring changes peer identities while preserving the incoming and outgoing degrees and each row’s signed weight multiset. Sign reassignment preserves the connections and weight magnitudes while changing relation signs. Within each trial, both interventions use the same observations at every perturbation level, allowing us to examine the effect of reference changes on the residual.

Figure 4 reports closure RMSE normalized by its unperturbed value within each trial on SMAP dataset. Across 1212 paired trials, the mean ratio reaches 1.2611.261 under rewiring and 1.3111.311 under sign reassignment at the largest perturbation level. These increases show that both peer identities and relation signs affect the residual, even when degrees or weight magnitudes are preserved. The two interventions are not budget-matched, so their ordering does not establish which aspect is more important. The results support the sensitivity of closure residuals to the relational reference, but do not by themselves establish relation-recovery accuracy or anomaly-detection performance.

4.4. Fusion-Weight Sensitivity

We examine how the balance between reconstruction and relation scoring affects detection performance. After branch standardization and softplus transformation calibrated on an independent normal sequence, we evaluate the fused score (1−α)​urec+α​ustr(1-\alpha)u^{\mathrm{rec}}+\alpha u^{\mathrm{str}} at 2121 weights. The detection threshold is recalibrated for each weight using the 9999th percentile of its normal scores. Figure 5 shows that intermediate fusion weights outperform either standalone branch for both processes on SMD dataset. At α=0.5\alpha=0.5, point F1 reaches 68.63%68.63\% and 55.71%55.71\% for Processes A and B, respectively, compared with 44.77%44.77\% and 37.37%37.37\% for their stronger standalone branches. This pattern is consistent with the two paths providing complementary evidence: intermediate weights retain contributions from both paths, whereas moving toward either endpoint reduces the contribution of one branch. The optimum is not necessarily symmetric. Process B peaks at α=0.4\alpha=0.4, with 56.55%56.55\% F1, exceeding equal-weight fusion by 0.840.84 percentage points. These results support equal weighting as an effective choice in the evaluated cases, while showing that the best balance can vary across processes.

4.5. Event Coverage Analysis

We distinguish detecting an event from covering its anomalous points. Figure 6 summarizes two event sets, labeled Populations A and B, each containing 3636 events on SMD dataset. Branch transformations and each rule’s 9999th-percentile threshold are calibrated on an independent normal sequence. Event coverage is the fraction of anomalous points within an event receiving an alarm, without point adjustment or event completion. Each curve reports the percentage of events whose coverage is at least the required level, weighting every event equally. Event retrieval requires strictly positive coverage, whereas all events qualify at a required coverage of zero. This metric measures the extent of coverage rather than the temporal continuity of alarms.

In Population A, equal-weight fusion detects at least one point in 2929 events, compared with 1818 for reconstruction and 2121 for relation scoring. It covers at least half the anomalous points in 1414 events, versus 77 for either branch. Population B shows a different tradeoff: fusion retrieves 2626 events, compared with 1818 for reconstruction and 1919 for relation scoring, yet reaches at least half coverage in only 44 events, compared with reconstruction’s 55. Detecting more events therefore need not imply higher within-event coverage. Separately, the observed normal-point alarm rate in Population A is 1.55%1.55\% under fusion, compared with 0.74%0.74\% and 1.29%1.29\% for reconstruction and relation scoring, respectively. These results show that event retrieval, within-event coverage, and false alarms capture distinct aspects of detection performance; improvements in one do not necessarily imply improvements in the others.

4.6. Ablation Study

Table 3 examines the two scoring paths and the learned basis memory. The single-path variants keep one path and omit the other; the raw-basis variant replaces the VQ codec with the original basis memory while retaining both scoring paths.

Adding relational scoring to reconstruction raises Aff-F1 from 69.9969.99 to 73.0773.07 on SWaT and from 78.1078.10 to 88.1388.13 on SMD. The full model also exceeds relation-only scoring by 4.994.99 and 12.3412.34 percentage points, respectively. The relational path is the weaker standalone detector here, yet removing it lowers both precision and recall, consistent with peer consistency acting as a complement rather than a replacement. Replacing VQ memory with raw bases lowers Aff-F1 by 1.501.50 and 7.607.60 percentage points on SWaT and SMD, respectively. Since this variant still supplies normal basis templates and retains both scoring paths, the gap suggests a benefit from learning the basis representation beyond simply providing normal temporal context. This comparison evaluates the encoder, codebook, and decoder jointly and does not isolate the contribution of quantization alone.

5. Conclusion

We revisited a premise of reconstruction-based anomaly detection, that difficulty of recovery tracks abnormality. A residual certifies that a window can be reproduced, and leaves undetermined whether its channels still explain one another.CLOSURE evaluates recoverability and cross-channel consistency through two separately learned prediction tasks on normal data. A diffusion reconstructor conditioned on a discrete memory of normal temporal bases assesses recoverability. A relation-closure operator assesses cross-channel consistency by predicting each channel from its peers. The target’s trajectory is withheld, and per-edge gates select the participating peers. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods across multiple benchmarks.

Appendices

Appendix A Baseline Descriptions

We summarize the methods appearing in the main comparison tables and experimental setup; the descriptions concern their modeling principles rather than a claim that their original evaluation protocols are identical.

  • •

    LOF (Breunig et al., 2000) compares an observation’s local density with those of its nearest neighbors and assigns a larger outlier score to observations in relatively sparse neighborhoods.

  • •

    iForest (Liu et al., 2012) isolates observations through random recursive partitions and scores points that require shorter isolation paths as more anomalous.

  • •

    CL-MPPCA (Tariq et al., 2019) combines convolutional LSTM modeling with mixtures of probabilistic principal component analyzers to capture temporal behavior and multiple normal operating patterns.

  • •

    TimesNet (Wu et al., 2022) reshapes a sequence into period-dependent two-dimensional tensors and uses convolutional blocks to model within-period and across-period variation.

  • •

    MTAD-GAT (Zhao et al., 2020) combines feature-wise and temporal graph attention with forecasting and reconstruction objectives to model dependencies across variables and time.

  • •

    LSTM-VAE (Park et al., 2018) models normal sequences with recurrent latent-variable encoding and decoding, using the resulting probabilistic reconstruction to assess anomalous observations.

  • •

    BeatGAN (Zhou et al., 2019) regularizes time-series reconstruction through adversarial training and identifies anomalous regions from discrepancies between observations and generated reconstructions.

  • •

    InterFusion (Li et al., 2021) uses a hierarchical variational model to capture inter-metric and temporal dependencies and evaluates observations through their reconstruction probabilities.

  • •

    DeepSVDD (Zhou et al., 2021) learns a representation concentrated around a normal-data center and detects anomalies from their distance to that center rather than reconstruction error.

  • •

    Anomaly Transformer (AnoTran) (Xu et al., 2021) contrasts a temporal prior association with learned series associations and combines their discrepancy with reconstruction evidence for detection.

  • •

    TranAD (Tuli et al., 2022) uses attention-based reconstruction with self-conditioning and adversarial training to model multivariate windows and score their reconstruction deviations.

  • •

    NPSR (Lai et al., 2024) combines point-wise and sequence-wise reconstruction to estimate nominality and condition anomaly scores on the distinction between point and contextual deviations.

  • •

    DCdetector (Yang et al., 2023) learns multiscale representations with an asymmetric dual-attention contrastive objective and derives detection evidence without a reconstruction objective.

  • •

    DiffAD (Xiao et al., 2023) detects anomalies through conditional diffusion-based imputation, progressively adjusting conditioning weights to preserve information from observed values.

  • •

    ImDiffusion (Chen et al., 2023) learns diffusion-based time-series imputers and uses their denoised estimates to measure departures from temporal and cross-variable context.

  • •

    D3R (Wang et al., 2023) combines dynamic decomposition with diffusion reconstruction to separate nonstationary drift from the deviations used for anomaly detection.

  • •

    OmniAnomaly (Su et al., 2019), also mentioned in the experimental setup, uses a stochastic recurrent model with a flexible variational posterior and reconstruction probabilities to detect multivariate anomalies.

Appendix B Datasets and Data Handling

B.1. Benchmark Descriptions

Server Machine Dataset (SMD).

SMD contains five weeks of monitoring data from 28 machines, with 38 recorded metrics per machine (Su et al., 2019). Its source release supplies separate training and test sequences and test anomaly annotations for each machine. Machine identities define separate sequences, not adjacent portions of one continuous trajectory.

Mars Science Laboratory (MSL).

MSL contains spacecraft telemetry from the Curiosity rover and expert-annotated anomalous intervals (Hundman et al., 2018). The source collection contains 27 telemetry streams. A stream’s model inputs include a monitored telemetry variable and encoded command context; these input columns should not all be interpreted as distinct physical sensors.

Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP).

SMAP is the companion NASA spacecraft collection with 55 telemetry streams and annotated anomalous intervals (Hundman et al., 2018). As in MSL, the monitored signal is accompanied by command-related inputs. The number of streams in the collection is distinct from the feature dimension of an individual input window.

Secure Water Treatment (SWaT).

SWaT records the operation of a six-stage water-treatment testbed through 51 sensor and actuator variables (Mathur and Tippenhauer, 2016). The commonly used release contains normal-operation data and a separate attack period. Measurements describe interacting processes such as flow, tank level, and valve operation, making cross-variable consistency relevant to monitoring.

Pooled Server Metrics (PSM).

PSM contains multivariate monitoring signals collected from eBay application servers (Abdulaal et al., 2021). The released training and test files describe server behavior through anonymized metrics, with anomaly labels supplied separately for testing. It complements SMD with a different operational environment and dependency structure.

GECCO.

The GECCO scenario in the NeurIPS time-series benchmark originates from drinking-water quality monitoring (Lai et al., 2021). It is named Water in the local release and contains nine measurement variables, including pH, temperature, and conductivity. Its annotations concern departures in a continuously monitored water-quality process.

Creditcard.

The Creditcard scenario contains transaction records with fraud annotations and is included in the same benchmark (Lai et al., 2021). The local release uses 29 transaction features. Unlike regularly sampled sensor measurements, consecutive observations represent transaction events; window position therefore describes event order rather than a fixed physical time interval.

Appendix C Algorithmic Details and Pseudocode

We detail the independent fitting of the basis codec, reconstructor, and sparse relation operator in Section 3, followed by calibration of their equal-weight score. The relational formulation assumes D≥2D\geq 2 retained channels. We write 𝒲q\mathcal{W}_{q} for the windows from segment q∈{tr,val,cal,test}q\in\{\mathrm{tr},\mathrm{val},\mathrm{cal},\mathrm{test}\} and store each input window together with its aligned detrended copy.

C.1. Fitting the Three Components

Basis codec.

For a normalized basis patch bb, let z=Eu​(b)z=E_{u}(b), c=cqu​(b)uc=c^{u}_{q_{u}(b)}, and b^=Du​(z+sg⁡[c−z])\widehat{b}=D_{u}(z+\operatorname{sg}[c-z]), as in Eq. 1. Each band minimizes the usual straight-through quantization objective (Van Den Oord et al., 2017):

(13) ℒVQu=𝔼b​[MSE⁡(b,b^)+MSE⁡(sg⁡[z],c)+βvq​MSE⁡(z,sg⁡[c])].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VQ}}^{u}=\mathbb{E}_{b}\!\left[\operatorname{MSE}(b,\widehat{b})+\operatorname{MSE}(\operatorname{sg}[z],c)+\beta_{\mathrm{vq}}\operatorname{MSE}(z,\operatorname{sg}[c])\right].

Here MSE\operatorname{MSE} averages squared coordinate differences, and βvq>0\beta_{\mathrm{vq}}>0 weights commitment to the selected code. The codebook loss updates the selected code vector, while the straight-through reconstruction gradient and commitment loss update the encoder. The fitted codecs and template indices are subsequently frozen. Each stored template retains paired high- and low-frequency code sequences; the two bands are read with the same template index.

Reconstruction and relation fitting.

The reconstructor minimizes ℒrec\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}} with the frozen memory. Independently, the relation predictor minimizes ℒrel\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rel}} over all retained targets. Its candidates comprise all D⁡(D−1)D(D-1) directed off-diagonal pairs, not just the nonzero entries of C0C_{0}. One hard-concrete gate vector is drawn per training minibatch; validation uses deterministic gates. The scored target set is not changed by pruning.

Appendix D Detailed Theoretical Analysis

We prove Lemma 3.1, Theorem 3.2, and Eq. 12, and derive the gate penalty. The results concern a frozen operator in fixed standardized coordinates. They do not imply that every anomaly violates its relations, that the branches are statistically independent, or that fusion improves detection. Nor does an empirical normal-data quantile guarantee a distribution-free false-alarm rate under dependence or distribution shift. Detection accuracy and event coverage require empirical evaluation.

D.1. Proof of the Normalization Lemma

Fix a row ii, let s=∑j|Ei​j|>0s=\sum_{j}|E_{ij}|>0, and take α>0\alpha>0 and ϵ>0\epsilon>0. Positive scaling preserves signs, so

(14) 𝒲ϵ​(α​E)i​j−𝒲0​(E)i​j\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{\epsilon}(\alpha E)_{ij}-\mathcal{W}_{0}(E)_{ij} =α​Ei​jα​s+ϵ−Ei​js\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha E_{ij}}{\alpha s+\epsilon}-\frac{E_{ij}}{s}
=−ϵ​Ei​js⁡(α​s+ϵ).\displaystyle=-\frac{\epsilon E_{ij}}{s(\alpha s+\epsilon)}.

Taking absolute values and summing over jj proves the exact identity

(15) ∑j|𝒲ϵ​(α​E)i​j−𝒲0​(E)i​j|=ϵ​∑j|Ei​j|s⁡(α​s+ϵ)=ϵα​s+ϵ.\sum_{j}\left|\mathcal{W}_{\epsilon}(\alpha E)_{ij}-\mathcal{W}_{0}(E)_{ij}\right|=\frac{\epsilon\sum_{j}|E_{ij}|}{s(\alpha s+\epsilon)}=\frac{\epsilon}{\alpha s+\epsilon}.

The right-hand side tends to zero when α​s/ϵ→∞\alpha s/\epsilon\to\infty, establishing Lemma 3.1. If ϵ=0\epsilon=0, every positive scaling gives exactly the same normalized row. The case s=0s=0 is excluded from the lemma because 𝒲0(E)i:\mathcal{W}_{0}(E)_{i:} is undefined; the implemented ϵ\epsilon-regularized map instead returns a zero row.

Why the order of gating matters.

Let si=∑j≠i|ωi​j|s_{i}=\sum_{j\neq i}|\omega_{ij}| and let mim_{i} be the absolute row mass after deterministic gating. Since 0≤g¯i​j≤10\leq\bar{g}_{ij}\leq 1,

(16) mi=∑j≠i|bi​j|​g¯i​j=∑j≠i|ωi​j|​g¯i​jsi+ϵ≤sisi+ϵ≤1.m_{i}=\sum_{j\neq i}|b_{ij}|\bar{g}_{ij}=\frac{\sum_{j\neq i}|\omega_{ij}|\bar{g}_{ij}}{s_{i}+\epsilon}\leq\frac{s_{i}}{s_{i}+\epsilon}\leq 1.

If all gates in a row equal c∈[0,1]c\in[0,1], its mass is c​si/(si+ϵ)cs_{i}/(s_{i}+\epsilon): the gates retain control over attenuation after normalization. A second exact normalization would remove this control because, for c>0c>0 and a nonzero row bi:b_{i:},

(17) c​bi​j∑k|c​bi​k|=bi​j∑k|bi​k|.\frac{cb_{ij}}{\sum_{k}|cb_{ik}|}=\frac{b_{ij}}{\sum_{k}|b_{ik}|}.

With a positive numerical stabilizer, cancellation is approximate when the row mass dominates that stabilizer, as quantified by the lemma. Normalization thus preserves relative contributions but not their absolute scale. This motivates separate attenuation parameters; it does not prove that learned sparsity necessarily improves detection.

D.2. Expected Gate Count and Deterministic Evaluation

For the hard-concrete gate in Eq. 6, assume Tg>0T_{g}>0 and γ<0<1<ζ\gamma<0<1<\zeta. The event gi​j>0g_{ij}>0 is unaffected by clipping at the upper endpoint. Writing u=ui​ju=u_{ij} and α=αi​j\alpha=\alpha_{ij} gives

(18) gi​j>0\displaystyle g_{ij}>0 ⇔σ⁡(log⁡u1−u+αTg)>−γζ−γ\displaystyle\iff\sigma\!\left(\frac{\log\frac{u}{1-u}+\alpha}{T_{g}}\right)>\frac{-\gamma}{\zeta-\gamma}
⇔log⁡u1−u>Tg​log⁡−γζ−α.\displaystyle\iff\log\frac{u}{1-u}>T_{g}\log\frac{-\gamma}{\zeta}-\alpha.

Because u∼𝒰⁡(0,1)u\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1), Pr⁡(log⁡u1−u≤x)=σ⁡(x)\Pr(\log\frac{u}{1-u}\leq x)=\sigma(x), and therefore

(19) πi​j:=Pr⁡(gi​j>0)=σ⁡(αi​j−Tg​log⁡−γζ),𝒮⁡(α)=1D⁡(D−1)​∑i≠jπi​j.\pi_{ij}:=\Pr(g_{ij}>0)=\sigma\!\left(\alpha_{ij}-T_{g}\log\frac{-\gamma}{\zeta}\right),\mathcal{S}(\alpha)=\frac{1}{D(D-1)}\sum_{i\neq j}\pi_{ij}.

This is the expected fraction of open candidate gates, following the hard-concrete relaxation of Louizos et al. (2017); it is not a confidence probability that an edge is physically correct. An open gate can still multiply a zero coefficient, so gate counts and nonzero effective-coefficient counts need not agree.

Validation and detection replace sampling by the deterministic surrogate

(20) g¯i​j=clip[0,1]⁡(γ+(ζ−γ)​σ​(αi​j)).\bar{g}_{ij}=\operatorname{clip}_{[0,1]}\left(\gamma+(\zeta-\gamma)\sigma(\alpha_{ij})\right).

The reference implementation uses Tg=2/3T_{g}=2/3, γ=−0.1\gamma=-0.1, and ζ=1.1\zeta=1.1. In general, g¯i​j≠𝔼⁡[gi​j]\bar{g}_{ij}\neq\mathbb{E}[g_{ij}]. Closing every incoming gate of target ii sets its prediction to zero, but its Huber loss remains in the objective; pruning cannot remove the target from supervision or scoring.

D.3. Proof of Target-Excluded Closure Response

Fix the fitted parameters, channel embeddings, and deterministic gates. Then target ii has the functional form

(21) Gi⋆(Z)=∑j≠iwi​j⋆ψϕ⋆(zj;vi⋆,vj⋆),zj=Z:,j.G_{i}^{\star}(Z)=\sum_{j\neq i}w_{ij}^{\star}\,\psi_{\phi^{\star}}(z_{j};v_{i}^{\star},v_{j}^{\star}),\qquad z_{j}=Z_{:,j}.

The weights and identity embeddings do not depend on the current observation. Let Z′=Z+δ​ei⊤Z^{\prime}=Z+\delta e_{i}^{\top}. For every j≠ij\neq i, Z′:,j=zjZ^{\prime}_{:,j}=z_{j}, hence every summand in Eq. 21 is unchanged and Gi⋆​(Z′)=Gi⋆​(Z)G_{i}^{\star}(Z^{\prime})=G_{i}^{\star}(Z). Subtracting predictions from observations yields

(22) Ei​(Z′)−Ei​(Z)\displaystyle E_{i}(Z^{\prime})-E_{i}(Z) =(zi+δ−Gi⋆​(Z′))−(zi−Gi⋆​(Z))\displaystyle=(z_{i}+\delta-G_{i}^{\star}(Z^{\prime}))-(z_{i}-G_{i}^{\star}(Z))
=δ.\displaystyle=\delta.

This proves both identities in Theorem 3.2. The argument is exact for nonlinear source messages and arbitrary perturbation magnitude. At differentiable points, the equivalent Jacobian statement is

(23) ∂Gi⋆∂zi=0L×L,∂Ei∂zi=IL.\frac{\partial G_{i}^{\star}}{\partial z_{i}}=0_{L\times L},\qquad\frac{\partial E_{i}}{\partial z_{i}}=I_{L}.

The result requires exclusion from the entire forward path, not just a zero diagonal in one matrix. A target-dependent gate, a shared all-channel feature mixer, or multihop feedback through another channel could invalidate the argument. None is present in the specified one-hop operator. A change to channel ii can still alter predictions for other targets, since it is allowed to serve as their source.

Signed response versus error magnitude.

The identity does not imply ‖Ei​(Z′)‖1>‖Ei​(Z)‖1\left\lVert E_{i}(Z^{\prime})\right\rVert_{1}>\left\lVert E_{i}(Z)\right\rVert_{1}. For example, choosing δ=−Ei​(Z)\delta=-E_{i}(Z) makes the new target residual zero. What always holds is

(24) ‖δ‖1−‖Ei​(Z)‖1≤‖Ei​(Z′)‖1≤‖δ‖1+‖Ei​(Z)‖1.\left\lVert\delta\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert E_{i}(Z)\right\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert E_{i}(Z^{\prime})\right\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert\delta\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert E_{i}(Z)\right\rVert_{1}.

Thus ‖δ‖1>2​‖Ei​(Z)‖1\left\lVert\delta\right\rVert_{1}>2\left\lVert E_{i}(Z)\right\rVert_{1} suffices to increase that target’s absolute residual, but a conclusion about all-channel aggregation additionally requires accounting for the other targets.

For an arbitrary Δ∈ℝL×D\Delta\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times D}, define

(25) U=Δ−(G⋆​(Z+Δ)−G⋆​(Z)),E′=E⁡(Z+Δ),E=E⁡(Z).U=\Delta-\bigl(G^{\star}(Z+\Delta)-G^{\star}(Z)\bigr),\qquad E^{\prime}=E(Z+\Delta),\quad E=E(Z).

|‖E′‖1,1−‖E‖1,1|\displaystyle\left|\left\lVert E^{\prime}\right\rVert_{1,1}-\left\lVert E\right\rVert_{1,1}\right| ≤‖E′−E‖1,1=‖U‖1,1.\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert E^{\prime}-E\right\rVert_{1,1}=\left\lVert U\right\rVert_{1,1}.

Division by L​DLD proves both inequalities in Eq. 12. In particular,

(27) 𝒟⁡(Z,Δ)−ℛ⁡(Z)≤ℛ⁡(Z+Δ)≤𝒟⁡(Z,Δ)+ℛ⁡(Z).\mathcal{D}(Z,\Delta)-\mathcal{R}(Z)\leq\mathcal{R}(Z+\Delta)\leq\mathcal{D}(Z,\Delta)+\mathcal{R}(Z).

If ℛ⁡(Z)≤ε0\mathcal{R}(Z)\leq\varepsilon_{0}, the perturbed residual lies within ε0\varepsilon_{0} of the unexplained perturbation magnitude. If 𝒟⁡(Z,Δ)>2​ℛ​(Z)\mathcal{D}(Z,\Delta)>2\mathcal{R}(Z), the lower bound is strictly larger than ℛ⁡(Z)\mathcal{R}(Z). Conversely, if 𝒟⁡(Z,Δ)≤η0\mathcal{D}(Z,\Delta)\leq\eta_{0}, the second inequality in Eq. 12 limits the change in residual magnitude to η0\eta_{0}, regardless of the size of Δ\Delta itself.

Linear special case.

For G⋆​(Z)=Z​W⊤G^{\star}(Z)=ZW^{\top}, the unexplained change becomes

(28) U=Δ⁡(I−W⊤).U=\Delta(I-W^{\top}).

Thus a perturbation satisfying Δ=Δ​W⊤\Delta=\Delta W^{\top} leaves the residual unchanged. In the nonlinear case, the corresponding condition is the finite-increment equality G⋆​(Z+Δ)−G⋆​(Z)=ΔG^{\star}(Z+\Delta)-G^{\star}(Z)=\Delta, not membership in a fixed linear subspace. These statements describe predictability under the learned operator, not a recovered causal graph or a universal definition of anomalous behavior.

D.5. Coordinates, Endpoint Ratios, and Decision Scope

Fixed standardized coordinates.

The perturbations above act on ZZ, after preprocessing. If a raw window is perturbed and then standardized again, the relevant change is the induced difference between the two standardized windows, not the raw additive perturbation. Channel-wise preprocessing preserves target exclusion from peer trajectories, but centering can remove an additive shift and rescaling can change its magnitude. Offline detrending also limits any claim about streaming detection delay.

The endpoint ratio is a different quantity.

Suppress the window index and set b=L−1​∑ℓ=1Lrℓb=L^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}r_{\ell}. For a second nonnegative residual profile r′r^{\prime}, write dL=rL′−rLd_{L}=r^{\prime}_{L}-r_{L} and db=L−1​∑ℓ(rℓ′−rℓ)d_{b}=L^{-1}\sum_{\ell}(r^{\prime}_{\ell}-r_{\ell}). The exact score difference is

(29) rL′b+db+ϵ−rLb+ϵ=dL​(b+ϵ)−rL​db(b+ϵ)​(b+db+ϵ).\frac{r^{\prime}_{L}}{b+d_{b}+\epsilon}-\frac{r_{L}}{b+\epsilon}=\frac{d_{L}(b+\epsilon)-r_{L}d_{b}}{(b+\epsilon)(b+d_{b}+\epsilon)}.

Both denominators are positive. Therefore an endpoint-error increase raises the ratio only when dL​(b+ϵ)>rL​dbd_{L}(b+\epsilon)>r_{L}d_{b}; a simultaneous increase in the background can offset it. Since b≥rL/Lb\geq r_{L}/L,

(30) 0≤rLb+ϵ<L,r1=⋯=rL=c>0⟹rLb+ϵ=cc+ϵ.0\leq\frac{r_{L}}{b+\epsilon}<L,\qquad r_{1}=\cdots=r_{L}=c>0\ \Longrightarrow\ \frac{r_{L}}{b+\epsilon}=\frac{c}{c+\epsilon}.

A uniformly large residual therefore produces a ratio near one, not a score proportional to its absolute magnitude. This readout emphasizes local departures within a window and does not measure how long an anomaly persists.
